report.source_text: After discontinuing antihistamines for 1 week, a water provocation test was administered. This involved regional contact using a damp cloth on the patient’s trunk, maintained at 35°C (figure 1A). After 20 min, there was a development of urticarial eruption on the trunk, which was consistent with the patient’s natural exposure to water (figure 1B).

report.source_text: At the 8-month follow-up, she did not report any further episodes of symptoms, unless a dosage of cetirizine was missed.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An early adolescent girl presented with a 2-year history of immediate-onset urticarial eruptions (pinpoint wheals with 1–3 cm erythematous flares) occurring exclusively upon contact with water at any temperature (shower, bath, pool, seawater, rain), with episodes lasting 30–60 minutes and spontaneous resolution. She also reported abdominal discomfort with drinking water and symptoms upon contact with animal saliva, but no symptoms with sweat or tears exposure. No systemic reactions (dyspnea, wheezing, dizziness, syncope) were documented. Routine laboratory evaluation (CBC, liver/renal function, urinalysis, immunoglobulin panels, thyroid function) was normal. A water provocation test at 35°C applied to the trunk for 20 minutes reproduced the urticarial eruption, confirming the diagnosis of aquagenic urticaria. The patient was treated with cetirizine 10 mg daily (after discontinuation of prior montelukast), resulting in substantial symptom relief. At 8-month follow-up, she remained symptom-free on cetirizine, with symptoms recurring only if doses were missed.
